input.question: How do hospitals dispose of donated blood/organs that go bad and can't be used anymore?
input.ground_truth: In some cases they don't. Back when I was a nuclear medicine intern I once saw an entire fridge filled with radioactive livers, some of which were many years old. The patients had been given radioactive medicine to help cure liver cancer, and in the cases when it didn't work and the patient died, they would have to remove the liver for safety reasons. Instead of spending the money to properly dispose of the radioactive waste (very expensive) the hospital just dumped them in an old fridge in the basement. This was at one of the top 10 hospitals in the US btw, not just some sketchy clinic.

Question: How do hospitals dispose of donated blood/organs that go bad and can't be used anymore?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine you have a special juice box that you saved for later, but after a while, it gets old and you can’t drink it anymore. Hospitals get special “juice boxes” called blood and organs that people kindly give to help others. But sometimes, the juice can’t be used because it gets old or isn’t good anymore.

When that happens, the hospital can’t give it to anyone. So, they have to get rid of it in a very safe way, so it doesn’t make anyone sick and doesn’t hurt the earth. They put it in special bags and take it to a place that knows exactly how to make it safe and clean it up. They don’t just throw it in the trash—they make sure it’s gone for good the right way!
